analysis.one_liner: Exempts professional employees of federal contractors from federal overtime pay rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to committee and then to a subcommittee, where it died at the end of the 104th Congress with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed the Fair Labor Standards Act, the law that requires overtime pay after 40 hours a week, so that professional employees working on federal contracts would no longer be entitled to overtime. That would lower labor costs for government contractors and subcontractors while taking overtime pay away from the affected workers. The bill was introduced by one representative, never attracted a single cosponsor, and died in a House subcommittee without any action or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal contractors and subcontractors would gain, because they could require long hours from professional employees on government contracts without paying time-and-a-half, reducing their labor costs and potentially making their bids on federal work more competitive.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new exemption to Section 13(b) of the Fair Labor Standards Act covering any professional employee of a federal contractor or subcontractor while working on a federal contract [S3].

The exemption would take effect immediately upon enactment and would apply retroactively, wiping out any pending overtime claims these workers had already filed, covering causes of action arising before, on, or after enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Professional employees working on federal contracts would lose their right to overtime pay under the Fair Labor Standards Act, meaning hours worked beyond 40 a week would no longer earn time-and-a-half. The retroactive clause would also erase any overtime claims they had already filed in court or were preparing to file.

drawbacks.text: Affected workers would lose overtime pay for hours beyond 40 per week, and the retroactive effective date would extinguish overtime claims that had already arisen before the law passed [S3].

The exemption is open-ended in scope: it covers 'any employee' in a 'professional capacity' on any federal contract, with details left to Secretary of Labor regulations, so its reach could grow over time beyond the workers originally contemplated [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit flows to contractors in the form of lower labor costs; the cost falls directly on the workers whose overtime pay disappears, and the retroactive provision would take away money those workers might already be owed. For the workers affected, this is a straightforward loss of pay protections with no compensating benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House education and labor committee, sent to a subcommittee a few weeks later, and then sat there until the Congress ended with no action and no vote.

narrative.text: Lindsey Graham introduced the bill in the House on March 14, 1996 [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities, which sent it to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections on March 29, 1996 [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractor workers came out ahead: their overtime protections and any pending overtime claims remained intact because the bill died. Contractors did not get the labor-cost savings the exemption would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal contractor workers kept their overtime rights

for.name: Lindsey Graham
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired in the 104th Congress
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections and took no further action, letting it die without a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican sponsored the bill with no cosponsors of either party, so no meaningful partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have let them avoid paying overtime to professional employees on federal contracts, cutting labor costs at those workers' expense. The retroactive clause would also have erased workers' pending overtime claims.
These workers would have lost their statutory right to time-and-a-half after 40 hours, and the retroactive effective date would have wiped out overtime claims already filed.
